card: Paper card. Question: Will trace interstitial impurities (oxygen and nitrogen) in Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloys continue to contribute positively to mechanical properties during long-term service, and will they affect phase stability or aid in phase segregation at in-service temperatures?. System: Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of high-purity elements, homogenization at 1200°C for 7 days followed by rapid cooling, and thermal aging at 700°C for durations of 1, 5, and 40 days.. Test conditions: Thermal aging at 700°C; nanoindentation with continuous stiffness measurement (CSM) at strain rate 0.05 s⁻¹; microstructural analysis via SEM, STEM, APT, EELS, and TKD.. Findings: The homogenized Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy exhibits a hardness of 5.05 GPa, which decreases to 4.22 GPa after 40 days of aging at 700°C, representing a 16% reduction.; Trace interstitials in the matrix decrease from 1.12 to 1.3 at % in the 1-day aged sample to 0.56 to 0.64 at % in the 40-day aged sample.; Intragranular precipitates form with a volume fraction of approximately 3% after 40 days of aging.; The precipitates are identified as α-Ti phase containing 73.7 at % Ti, 18.3 at % O, and 5.88 at % N.; The calculated lattice distortion parameter (δ) decreases by approximately 17.6% when oxygen content drops from 1.2 at % to 0.6 at %.; Precipitates with a 3% volume fraction contribute only 217.48 MPa (5.15%) to the overall nanoindentation hardness.; Precipitate-free zones (PFZs) of approximately 3 μm width form adjacent to grain boundaries due to solute depletion.; The precipitates obey the Burgers orientation relationship: (0002)HCP ǁ {110}BCC and [112¯0]HCP ǁ <111>BCC.. Mechanism: Trace interstitials (O and N) initially provide solid solution strengthening; upon aging, they partition to form α-Ti precipitates, depleting the matrix of these interstitials. This depletion reduces lattice distortions and solid solution strengthening, causing softening that outweighs the minimal hardening contribution from the 3% volume fraction of precipitates.. Limitations: The study notes that quantifying solid solution strengthening in HEAs is challenging due to the inability to distinguish between solvent and solute atoms, and that the theoretical hardening calculations assume equal volume fractions for different precipitate morphologies.. Future work: The authors suggest exploring ways to strike a dynamic balance between hardening from aging precipitates and softening from reduced solid solution strengthening, and emphasize the need to better control oxygen and nitrogen levels during processing for industrial applications.. Quote: "Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging."

card: Paper card. Question: Do high-entropy alloys (HEAs) possess unique irradiation damage resistance mechanisms compared to conventional alloys, and what are the specific roles of thermal conductivity, defect mobility, and defect energetics in this behavior?. System: Concentrated solid-solution alloys and HEAs (defined as alloys with ≥5 components at 5–35 at.%) including NiFe, NiCo, NiCoCrFe, CrFeCoNi, Ni0.8Fe0.2, Ni0.8Cr0.2, Fe-Cr, Fe-Ni, and CrFeCoNiMn; compared against pure Ni, pure Fe, and conventional austenitic steels.. Processing: Not stated (Review of existing literature and atomistic simulations; no new processing described).. Test conditions: Irradiation with energetic neutrons (≥1 MeV), protons, or heavy ions; temperatures ranging from room temperature to high homologous temperatures (T/Tm > 0.2); damage levels up to 250 dpa; PKA energies ≥10 keV; specific mention of 14.1 MeV fusion neutrons and Gen-IV fission conditions (>600 °C).. Findings: MD studies on NiFe (lower thermal conductivity) found significantly fewer stable Frenkel pair (FP) defects after cascades at PKA energies ≥10 keV compared to pure Ni.; In CrFeCoNi, void swelling was negligible between 16 and 54 dpa, with significant swelling only observed at high doses of 86–250 dpa.; Defect clusters in concentrated Ni binaries were found to be smaller and more numerous than in pure Ni at room temperature, attributed to slower defect mobilities.; Damage accumulation in pure Ni saturates earlier, whereas damage in concentrated alloys accumulates more slowly but may peak at a higher level at higher doses.; Void swelling in concentrated alloys is often suppressed by over an order of magnitude compared to pure metals at the same damage level.; Atomistic simulations show a distribution of migration energies in concentrated alloys, with average migration energies for interstitials being higher than in pure Ni.; A comprehensive review by Dąbrowa and Danielewski found no conclusive experimental evidence that thermally-induced diffusion is sluggish in HEAs compared to conventional alloys.; Some studies suggest HEAs may be 'self-healing' due to rapid recrystallization following cascade-induced amorphization caused by high inter-atomic stress levels.. Mechanism: The authors describe a complex interplay of mechanisms: (1) Reduced thermal conductivity in HEAs leads to more localized thermal spikes, potentially allowing more FP recombination; (2) Sluggish defect mobilities (due to variable chemical environments and lattice distortion) reduce the migration of interstitials, bringing their mobility closer to vacancies, which suppresses void swelling and radiation-induced segregation; (3) Higher vacancy formation energies and distribution of defect formation energies in concentrated alloys contribute to void suppression; (4) High inter-atomic stresses may facilitate amorphization followed by rapid recrystallization ('self-healing').. Limitations: The authors state that understanding of HEA irradiation responses remains in its infancy, with many proposed mechanisms (sluggish diffusion, lattice distortion) being unconvincing or not universally applicable. There is a lack of systematic studies comparing FCC, BCC, and HCP metals under identical conditions, and no conclusive experimental evidence for abnormally sluggish diffusion or lattice distortion in stable HEAs.. Future work: The authors highlight the need for more work to match the understanding of HEAs to that of conventional alloys, specifically calling for systematic studies comparing different crystal structures under the same irradiation conditions, and distinguishing between changes in defect migration energies versus formation energies during irradiation.. Quote: "It is found that our understanding of the irradiation responses of HEAs remains in its infancy, and much work is needed in order for our knowledge of any single HEA system to match our understanding of conventional alloys such as austenitic steels."

Paper card. Question: Do High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) possess enhanced intrinsic damage resistance versus conventional alloys under irradiation, and what are the specific mechanisms or limitations governing their phase stability and mechanical response?. System: Al0.3CoCrFeNi, Al0.12NiCoFeCr, TiZrNbHfTa, CrFeNi-based alloys, CrFeMnCoNi, BCC refractory HEAs (Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ta, W combinations), Fe-Ni-Mn-Cr, Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic alloys, 316 stainless steel, 316H stainless steel, 304 stainless steel, RAFM steel, MoNbTiTaW, CoCrFeNiPd, FeCuCrMnMo. Processing: Not stated (text reviews existing studies involving thin films, nanocrystalline materials, arc melting, spark plasma sintering, and various irradiation conditions including He-irradiation, electron irradiation, and ion/neutron irradiation). Test conditions: Irradiation at room temperature and 300-500 °C; thermal annealing at irradiation temperatures; damage levels up to many dpa; thin film and nanocrystalline conditions; He-irradiation; electron irradiation. Findings: In Al0.3CoCrFeNi, ballistic mixing suppressed precipitation at lower temperatures while radiation-enhanced diffusion enhanced it at higher temperatures.; In Al0.12NiCoFeCr, irradiation led to decomposition of the single phase solid solution, whereas longer thermal exposure at 500 °C did not.; Moschetti et al. found a small increase (~10%) in nanohardness, yield strength, and ultimate-tensile strength for He-irradiated TiZrNbHfTa with no loss of ductility.; CrFeNi-based alloys showed significant hardening similar to 316 stainless steel, unlike BCC refractory HEAs which showed no or very limited hardening.; A sigma to BCC transition at room temperature has been observed in some alloys, which is very unlikely to have been favourable in the non-irradiated state.; The dose needed for damage saturation in an Fe-Ni-Mn-Cr alloy was found to be comparable to that in more conventional Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic alloys at 500 °C.; Microstructural evolution and irradiation hardening in some FCC HEAs was found to be similar to 316H stainless steel at 300 °C.; CrFeMnCoNi retained more hydrogen than 304 and 316 L steels but showed only marginal ductility decrease after gaseous charging.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the disparity in responses between BCC and FCC HEAs may be due to the distribution of migration energies for vacancies and interstitials exhibiting a much larger overlap in BCC HEAs, leading to enhanced defect recombination. They suggest that compositional complexity might uniquely enable effects such as poor thermal conductivities affecting cascade dynamics (reducing FPs formed) and a spread in defect formation energies (potentially higher vacancy formation energies).. Limitations: Many studies fail to assess alloys under conditions that appropriately probe resistance to irradiation damage, such as using thin films where defects annihilate at surfaces, nanocrystalline materials with many boundaries, irradiation at room temperature where defect mobility is inhibited, or electron irradiation which does not cause the same damage as ions or neutrons. Additionally, there is a lack of comparison to conventional alloys or less compositionally-complex alloys assessed under the same conditions.. Future work: Further investigation is needed into the disparity in responses of BCC vs. FCC HEAs, the influence of diffusion and lattice distortion, the effect of reduced thermal conductivities on cascade dynamics, and the defect energetics in BCC refractory HEAs. Design efforts require tuning compositions to optimize defect formation energies, sink strengths, and biases using advanced atomic-scale models.. Quote: "ballistic mixing suppressed precipitation in irradiated areas in comparison to non-irradiated regions, but radiation-enhanced diffusion was found to enhance it at higher temperatures"

card: Paper card. Question: What are the physical origins of the exceptional high-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs)?. System: NbTaTiV (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at.%) and CrMoNbV (nominal CrMoNbV at.%); search space includes the 10-component Al-Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr family.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt.% purity elements under argon atmosphere followed by drop-casting into cylindrical rods; NbTaTiV homogenized at 1473 K for 3 days then water-cooled; CrMoNbV tested in the as-cast state.. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at strain rates of 1 × 10−3 s−1 (NbTaTiV) and 2 × 10−4 s−1 (CrMoNbV); temperatures up to 1173 K; in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) performed during deformation.. Findings: Neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis yielded q values of -0.6 to -0.4 for NbTaTiV and -2 for CrMoNbV, consistent with edge dislocations and distinct from screw dislocations (+1.9 to +2.1).; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of NbTaTiV deformed at 293 K showed 75% (58 of 77) of dislocations were of edge character.; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of CrMoNbV deformed at 293 K showed 56% (23 of 41) of dislocations were of edge character.; At 1173 K, edge dislocations remained dominant with 82% (27 of 33) in NbTaTiV and 64% (81 of 127) in CrMoNbV.; The CrMoNbV alloy exhibited the highest reported strength at a homologous temperature of 1173 K.; A computationally guided search over 10^7 BCC HEA compositions identified over 10^6 possible ultra-strong high-temperature alloy compositions.; Theoretical predictions for NbTaTiV strength were lower than experimental values by ~300-500 MPa, attributed to 1.6 at.% O+N interstitial impurities.. Mechanism: In complex HEAs, fluctuations in local solute arrangements create large local variations in potential energy, forcing edge dislocations to adopt a low-energy wavy structure; plastic flow requires thermal activation to overcome large energy barriers created by adjacent high-energy environments, enabling high strength retention at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The theory does not capture the strength plateau observed at 973–1273 K in many BCC HEAs; neutron pattern quality for CrMoNbV was lower than for NbTaTiV, especially at low plastic strains; the theory assumes a homogeneous average alloy which may not fully capture local complexities.. Future work: Propose fabrication and testing of specific alloys (Mo5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo6WCrZrHf, Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf) with predicted strengths of ~2.5-3 GPa at 1300 K; combine design strategy with detailed thermodynamics and high ductility criteria to discover multi-objective alloys.. Quote: "Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations."

card: Paper card. Question: How can massive amounts of interstitial elements (O, C, N) be dissolved in a metallic host lattice without forming brittle ceramic phases, while simultaneously achieving near-theoretical strength and large deformability?. System: TiNbZr-O-C-N massive interstitial solid solution (MISS) alloys, specifically (TiNbZr)86O12C1N1 (at%) referred to as O-12 MISS alloy, and reference alloys (TiNbZr)92O6C1N1 (O-6), (TiNbZr)92O8 (O-8), and equiatomic TiNbZr. Processing: Magnetron sputtering on Si (001) substrates with Ar pressure of 0.3 Pa and substrate bias power of 90 W, followed by annealing in a vacuum (10−2 Pa) at 500 °C for 2 h to promote interstitial diffusion. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression of micropillars (diameter 1.0–1.6 μm) at ambient temperature with a nominal strain rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1; in-situ SEM bending and tensile tests at ambient temperature. Findings: The O-12 MISS alloy contains 12 at% interstitial O with no oxides, carbides, or nitrides formed.; The alloy exhibits an ultrahigh compressive yield strength of 4.2 ± 0.2 GPa.; The alloy maintains large deformability of 65% strain at ambient temperature without localized shear deformation.; The shear stress ratio τy/G reaches 1/18, approaching the theoretical limit of ~1/10.; In bending tests, the O-12 alloy shows an ultrahigh flow stress of 5.6 ± 0.5 GPa and withstands a tensile strain of 54%.; Grain refinement occurs during deformation, reducing grain diameters from 20–50 nm to 5–20 nm at ~65% strain.; C and N segregate to grain boundaries with concentrations of 1.8 ± 0.3 at% and 1.0 ± 0.2 at%, respectively.; The elastic modulus (E) of the O-12 alloy is 95 GPa, while the shear modulus (G) is calculated to be 38 GPa.. Mechanism: Massive interstitial O atoms create strong, asymmetrical lattice distortions that impede dislocation nucleation and motion, while C and N segregation to grain boundaries reduces interfacial energy, stabilizing the boundaries against coarsening and suppressing localized shear deformation; this combination promotes dislocation multiplication and grain refinement without softening.. Limitations: The study notes that thermodynamic calculations cannot fully consider lattice distortions and interstitial site variations in concentrated solid solutions, and that Ga+ ion beam milling could potentially alter surface layers, though this was minimized.. Future work: The authors propose that the MISS alloy design strategy is applicable to a wide range of materials including alloys with multiple principal elements and may provide fundamental insights into plastic deformation in massive interstitially doped solid solutions.. Quote: "Here we introduce a class of massive interstitial solid solution (MISS) alloys by using a highly distorted substitutional host lattice, which enables solution of massive amounts of interstitials as an additional principal element class, without forming ceramic phases."

card: Paper card. Question: Can microwave-synthesized FeCoNiMnCu high entropy alloy (HEA) coatings on SS-304 steel enhance surface hardness, thermostability, and tribo-corrosion resistance for use in solid oxide fuel-cell (SOFC) interconnects?. System: Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA coating on SS-304 stainless steel substrate. Processing: Ball-milling of Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu powders (20 wt% each) at 200 rpm with a 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio; preheating at 100°C for 24 h; microwave hybrid heating (MHH) using a multimode applicator at 900 W and 2.45 GHz with charcoal as a susceptor; thermal exposure in air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C. Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers tester (ASTM E384); corrosion tested by immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl for 120 h (ASTM G44); wear tested via pin-on-disc (ASTM G99) at 2 m/s sliding speed, 1000 m distance, and 15 N axial load; microstructure analyzed via SEM and XRD. Findings: Average hardness increased from 210 HV (SS-304) to 325 HV (coated), representing a 54.76% improvement.; Corrosion weight loss of the 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu coating was 0.3004 mg after 120 h in 3.5 wt% NaCl.; A protective Cr2O3 layer and a high-entropy spinel coating of (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 formed after thermal exposure at 800 °C for 10 weeks.; XRD analysis identified phases including Fe, FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Mn2O3, (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4, and Cr2O3.; SEM images revealed a uniform cladding distribution with homogeneity in the interfacial layer.; The cladding demonstrated remarkable stability under thermal expansion studies, withstanding significant volume variations at elevated temperatures.. Mechanism: The formation of harder phases (FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Mn2O3) during microwave cladding contributes to raised hardness. During thermal exposure, alloy elements react with atmospheric oxygen to form protective Cr2O3 and (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 layers, which act as barriers against further oxidation, corrosion, and wear.. Limitations: Some cracks were observed between the cladding layer and substrate, attributed to differential cooling rates, residual stresses, and inadequate bonding.. Future work: Optimize microwave cladding parameters including temperature, metallic powder content, environmental conditions, irradiation duration, pre-heating time, separators, and susceptors to further enhance effectiveness.. Quote: "The deposited steel with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu high entropy alloy (HEA) was exposed to thermal-exposure in the air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C."

Paper card. Question: Can a microwave-synthesized Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 high-entropy alloy coating enhance the surface hardness, wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability of SS-304 steel for SOFC interconnect applications?. System: SS-304 steel substrate coated with a mixture of 20% Fe, 20% Co, 20% Ni, 20% Mn, and 20% Cu (Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA). Processing: Microwave cladding using microwave energy to deposit the HEA powder onto the SS-304 surface. Test conditions: Corrosion exposure: 3.5 wt.% NaCl media and air exposure for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C; Wear testing: Sliding speed of 2 m/s, sliding distance of 1000 m, and load of 15 N; Thermal expansion test: 1200 °C for 72 h duration in a muffle-furnace. Findings: Hardness of SS-304 was raised by approximately 54.76% after coating.; Wear rate of the coated sample was measured at 0.0018 mm3/m.; Coefficient of friction for the coated steel was determined to be 0.2.; Corrosion loss was reduced after thermal exposure in air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C.; Thermal expansion test showed only a 1 mm3 variation in volume after exposure to 1200 °C for 72 h.; Protective Cr2O3 layer and high-entropy spinel coating of (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4 formed after thermal exposure.; Harder phases including Fe, FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Fe2O3, and Mn2O3 were observed after microwave cladding.. Mechanism: The alloying components (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu) serve as sacrificial anodes to shield the underlying steel and help form stable oxide scales. High-temperature exposure aids in the development of protective oxide scales that function as barriers to retard the diffusion of corrosive species. The enhanced hardness is attributed to the formation of distinct harder phases such as Fe, FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Fe2O3, and Mn2O3.. Limitations: The text notes that dark spots on the corroded surface indicate localized corrosion where the coating may have been breached or performed less well due to flaws or microstructural alterations. The study also implies that electrical conductivity and area-specific resistance were not fully characterized in this specific work.. Future work: Emphasis must be contemplated on analyzing the electrical-conductivity for SOFCs interconnects applications. Emphasis must be centered on analyzing the oxidation-resistance and area-specific resistance in simulated service environments. Additional characterizations must be contemplated on the coatings before and after thermal exposure in air at 800°C. The cross-section of the coatings has been assessed to affirm the continuous and protective (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 coating.. Quote: "The hardness has been ameliorated by about 54.76%."

W4390430670.title: Unveiling of grain structure, porosity, phase distributions, microstructural morphology, surface hardness, and tribo-corrosion characteristics of nickel, and titanium dioxide-based SS-304 steel microwave composite coatings cladding

card: Paper card. Question: How does the sequence of oxidation and phase transformations in FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder differ between HVOF deposition, continuous heating, and isothermal annealing, and how do these processes influence the resulting coating properties?. System: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder (gas-atomized). Processing: High-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying using Hipojet 2700M, MP-2100, PF-3350; continuous heating in air at 20°/min up to 1400 °C; isothermal annealing at 800 °C for 1, 9, and 27 hours. Test conditions: Spraying distances of 150 mm to 250 mm; heating rates of 20°/min; annealing at 800 °C in air; microhardness tested at 50 g load for 10 s. Findings: In gas-atomized state, the powder consists of a BCC supersaturated solid solution with a small B2 peak.; Increasing spraying distance from 150 mm to 250 mm increases oxide content but decreases microhardness from 750 HV to 550 HV.; Under HVOF spraying, oxidation develops prior to the decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution.; During continuous heating, sigma phase formation begins at 650 °C, while α-Al2O3 reflexes appear at 1050 °C.; Under isothermal annealing at 800 °C, BCC decomposition with sigma formation occurs earlier than pronounced oxidation.; After annealing for 27 h at 800 °C, microhardness reaches 910 HV due to sigma phase formation.; Al-depleted BCC zones transform to FCC phase during HVOF spraying, whereas a sigma 'shell' forms around particles during annealing.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the extremely high heating and cooling rates during HVOF spraying prevent sigma phase formation, allowing oxidation to deplete aluminum from the BCC lattice before decomposition, which destabilizes the BCC structure and causes a transformation to FCC. In contrast, during annealing, the slower kinetics allow the supersaturated BCC solid solution to decompose into sigma phase before significant oxidation occurs; the subsequent aluminum outflow to the surface oxide layer then influences the remaining core composition and phase stability.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that higher oxide content does not result in higher microhardness due to increased porosity and soft FCC phase formation.. Future work: The authors propose that feedstock powder with excessive Al concentration should be used to prevent FCC formation during deposition, and that preliminary heat treatment of the feedstock powder allows obtaining powder with higher hardness and a protective alumina shell.. Quote: "High temperature and high oxygen concentration in spraying lead to oxidation development prior to supersaturated solid solution decomposition."

card: Paper card. Question: How do powder preparation, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), and microplasma spraying (MPS) affect the phase composition and microstructure of FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 high entropy alloy, and what are the effects of subsequent annealing on these properties?. System: FeNiCoCrAl1.3Mo0.5 (nominal composition FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3). Processing: Gas atomization (1600 °C melt, 40 bar argon pressure, ~25 μm particles); L-PBF (190 W laser power, 1000 mm/s scanning speed, 100 μm spot size, 40 μm layer thickness, N2 atmosphere); MPS (38 V, 2.3 L/min plasma Ar, 2 L/min carrying Ar, 26 A current); Annealing (600 °C and 900 °C for 1 h in air). Test conditions: XRD (20°–140° 2Θ, 2°/min), SEM/EDS, DTA (20°/min to 900 °C), Vickers microhardness (50 g load, 10 s dwell), Nanoindentation (1500 μN load, 8×8 matrix). Findings: Gas atomization produces a supersaturated BCC solid solution with Mo-rich segregations on dendrite peripheries.; L-PBF samples exhibit microstructure and phase composition very similar to the as-atomized powder.; MPS coatings contain a fraction of FCC phase due to Al oxidation and subsequent Al-depletion regions.; Maximum microhardness of 950 HV is achieved in powder and L-PBF samples after annealing at 600 °C.; After annealing at 900 °C, microhardness decreases to approximately 850 HV due to stress relaxation and σ-phase precipitation.; The elastic modulus of the L-PBF sample is 165 GPa, which is 12% lower than that of the cast alloy (186 GPa).; Annealing at 900 °C causes decomposition of the solid solution into B2 and σ-phases.; High-temperature annealing (900 °C) of MPS coatings leads to sample failure due to oxide growth and stress development.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the hardness increase at 600 °C to the growth of elastic stresses between multiple BCC solid solutions caused by increased element segregation. The subsequent decrease at 900 °C is explained by stress relaxation from solid solution decomposition, counterbalanced by the precipitation of hard, homogeneously distributed σ-phase. In MPS coatings, Al oxidation creates Al-depleted regions where the FCC structure becomes thermodynamically stable compared to BCC.. Limitations: The authors note that the absence of the μ-phase in the cast alloy, despite Thermo-Calc predictions, may be due to extremely low formation rates or insufficient database reliability. Additionally, high-temperature annealing of MPS coatings resulted in partial destruction, limiting the evaluation of their high-temperature stability.. Quote: "Maximum hardness (950 HV) is achieved in the powder and L-PBF samples after annealing at 600 °C."

card: Paper card. Question: How do atomic interactions and Ti content influence the order–disorder transition and phase stability in FCC-type FeCoNiAl1−xTix high-entropy alloys?. System: FeCoNiAl1−xTix (specifically Fe25Co25Ni25Al25−xTix) with Ti content ranging from 0 to 9 at.%. Processing: First-principles calculations using DFT (VASP, PAW method, PBE functional, 500 eV plane waves, 3×3×3 supercells) to determine atomic interactions; Thermodynamic Monte Carlo simulations (62,500 atoms, 2300 K to 300 K, 4000 steps equilibration); CALPHAD simulations using Thermo-Calc 2021b with TCHEA5 database and Sheil–Gulliver model.. Test conditions: Simulated temperatures from 2300 K down to 300 K; Ti concentrations of 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 at.% (replacing Al); ferromagnetic state for Ni, Fe, Co.. Findings: The order–disorder transition temperature for equal-atomic AlCoFeNi HEAs was calculated at 1650 K.; The order–disorder transition temperature decreased with increasing Ti content: 1644 K (1 at.% Ti), 1638 K (3 at.% Ti), 1632 K (5 at.% Ti), and 1574 K (7 at.% Ti).; CALPHAD predicted L12 precipitation temperatures of 1600 K, 1540 K, 1490 K, and 1465 K for alloys with 1, 3, 5, and 7 at.% Ti, respectively.; Ni3Al and Ni3Ti were identified as the most stable L12 intermetallics with formation enthalpies of −0.44 eV and −0.47 eV, respectively.; Co atoms accumulate and segregate at the interfaces of precipitates due to weak Co–Co atomic interactions (less than 0.03 eV).; Strain-induced interactions are significant for Al–X pairs due to the small atomic radius of Al (1.25 Å).; Laves phase precipitation was predicted to begin at approximately 1300 K when Ti content is large enough.; The simulated precipitate sizes in AlCoFeNi HEAs were found to be not greater than 35 nm.. Mechanism: Atomic ordering is driven by repulsive nearest-neighbor interactions and strong strain-induced interactions caused by atomic size mismatch, particularly involving Al. The formation of L12 precipitates (Ni3Al, Ni3Ti, Fe3Al) is governed by the negative formation enthalpies of these intermetallics. Ti addition stabilizes the L12 phase thermodynamically but lowers the transition temperature, while Co atoms segregate at interfaces due to negligible interaction energies with other species.. Limitations: The authors state that 'some disagreements between the CALPHAD simulated results based on the current databases and Monte Carlo as well as experimental results are still present' and that 'the severe lattice distortion caused by Ti alloying significantly changed the atomic configuration, which is a sensitive parameter for Monte Carlo simulations'. They also note that 'the order–disorder transition in FeCoNiAl1−xTix HEAs is complicated' involving site occupation and phase competition not fully covered.. Future work: The authors propose that 'the modulation of the Ti content would be an effective way to affect the microstructure and mechanical properties' and suggest that 'an investigation into the higher Ti content... would be an interesting subject for future investigations'. They also state that 'the site occupation in the L12 phase was found to be complex, and it requires further study'.. Quote: "The order–disorder transition temperatures decrease with increasing Ti content in FeCoNiAl1−xTix high-entropy alloys"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the pore structure of rare-earth-zirconate high-entropy ceramics be regulated to achieve low thermal conductivity and high compressive strength for thermal insulation applications?. System: (La0.25Eu0.25Gd0.25Yb0.25)2(Zr0.75Ce0.25)2O7. Processing: Tert-butyl alcohol (TBA)-based gel-casting method; initial solid loadings of 5–15 vol%; sintering at 1500 °C for 2 h after debinding at 620 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Room temperature to 1200 °C; compressive strength testing at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; porosity via Archimedes' method; thermal conductivity via laser method (LFA-1000). Findings: Porous high-entropy ceramics exhibited a single fluorite phase without impurity phases.; Porosity ranged from 67.1% to 81.5% as solid loading increased from 15 vol% to 5 vol%.; Compressive strength increased from 1.02 ± 0.61 MPa to 6.45 ± 1.76 MPa with increasing solid loading.; Room temperature thermal conductivity ranged from 0.0642 to 0.1213 W/(m·K).; The sample with 81.5% porosity showed a thermal conductivity of 0.1467 W/(m·K) at 1200 °C.; Average pore size decreased from 1.63 μm to 1.19 μm as solid loading increased from 5 vol% to 10 vol%.; Grain size was approximately 1 μm with uniform and irregular pore opening structures.. Mechanism: The unique pore structure with micron size (1–2 μm) impedes heat propagation by scattering electromagnetic waves corresponding to the peak of radiant heat transfer (1.6–2.9 μm) according to Mie scattering law, while high porosity reduces convective and conductive heat transfer through air-filled pores.. Limitations: The experimental results do not completely fit the Effective Medium Theory (EMT) model, likely due to uneven distribution of pore size; the Maxwell–Eucken equation is insufficient because it lacks consideration of heat transport when phases are continuous.. Future work: The authors state that rare-earth-zirconate porous high-entropy ceramics with tailored pore structures are expected to be thermal insulation materials, implying further development of tailored structures for high-temperature applications.. Quote: "The regulation of pore structures was realized through changing different initial solid loadings."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the high-temperature tensile mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 refractory high-entropy alloy, and can a constitutive model predict its flow behavior?. System: NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 (Refractory High-Entropy Alloy). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (5–8 remelts), drop-casting into water-cooled copper mold, cold rolling (50% thickness reduction), stress-relief annealing (800 °C, 10 min), and water quenching.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 298–1027 K (up to 1273 K mentioned in abstract) with strain rates of 0.001–0.1 s⁻¹; infrared heating with 5 min hold; samples coated with boron nitride paint.. Findings: At 473 K, the alloy exhibited a tensile ductility of 12%.; In the 673–873 K range, yield strength remained above 800 MPa while ductility was reduced.; A 'high-temperature plateau' in strength was observed between 873 K and 1073 K where strength changes were negligible.; At 1223 K, plasticity rose to more than 30% while yield strength decreased significantly.; Nanoindentation revealed a uniform nanohardness of 5.13 ± 0.01 GPa across dendritic and interdendritic regions.; Deformation was controlled by dislocation slip with no evidence of deformation twins.; The deformation activation energy (Q) was calculated to be 379 kJ/mol.; The hyperbolic sine constitutive model predicted peak stress with a maximum error of about 100 MPa.. Mechanism: Plastic deformation is controlled by dislocation slip, where the morphology and density of dislocations dictate mechanical properties. The high-temperature strength plateau is attributed to a competition between work hardening (dislocation accumulation) and softening mechanisms (dynamic recovery or recrystallization), while the unusual strength retention is speculated to involve edge dislocations acting as barriers via thermal super-jogging.. Limitations: The study notes that the mechanism for the retained strength at high temperatures is currently unknown and that the observed low-plasticity plateau between 873 K and 1073 K contradicts general alloy experience; potential causes like dynamic oxygen embrittlement or nanoscale precipitation were considered but not fully confirmed.. Future work: The authors propose that the potential nanoscale precipitates responsible for ductility loss at 1073 K, which were too small to be seen in TEM, will be the subject of another study.. Quote: "At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: What alloying and scaling conditions lead to the strongest both ductile and stable materials?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) thin films and pillars. Processing: d.c. magnetron co-sputtering on (100) silicon or sapphire substrates at room temperature; Ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) used with 1.2 keV beam energy, 5 mA current, and 35° incidence angle to reduce grain size; Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) used to mill pillars with diameters of ~1 μm, 500, 200, and 100 nm. Test conditions: Microcompression tests at a strain rate of 2 × 10−3 s−1; Thermal annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days in argon atmosphere. Findings: HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ~10 GPa, one order of magnitude higher than the bulk form.; Compressive plastic strains over 30% were achieved in smaller pillars without cracking.; 580-nm Normal HEA pillars show a yield strength of ~5 GPa, while 580-nm IBAD HEA pillars reach ~6.5 GPa.; Smallest IBAD HEA pillars (~70–100 nm diameter) exhibit yield strengths of ~8–10 GPa.; After annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days, HEA pillars retain a high yield strength of ~5 GPa, whereas pure W films show significant grain growth and pore formation.; IBAD HEA pillars exhibit a log–log slope of −0.2 for the relationship between flow stress and pillar diameter, indicating the lowest size dependence among reported pillars.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is attributed to the simultaneous operation of four strengthening mechanisms: lattice friction, Taylor hardening, source-controlled strength, and grain-boundary strengthening. The excellent thermal stability is attributed to relatively low grain-boundary energy due to the highly disordered grain interiors in HEAs, which lowers the driving force for grain-boundary migration compared to pure metals.. Limitations: The text notes that large pillars (>1 μm) experience cracking at strains larger than ~20% and that the smallest pillars (~70–100 nm) show higher scattering levels in strength due to inhomogeneous distribution of grain boundaries.. Future work: The authors state that mechanical tests for small-scale HEAs at high temperatures are still needed to prove their capability as high-temperature materials, and that further work is required to optimize small-scale HEAs for applications, such as determining the best alloying elements and optimized grain and specimen size combinations.. Quote: "Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (atomic %). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.. Findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.; Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.; Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).; The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).; Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.; Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.; Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.. Limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.. Future work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.. Quote: "Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a hierarchical microstructure be induced in a single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA) to achieve superior high-temperature tensile yield strength and ductility compared to advanced single crystal superalloys?. System: Ni48.3Co16.9Al10.2Fe8.9Cr7.4Ti5.8Nb1.2Mo0.9W0.4 (at.%) single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA). Processing: Bridgman casting of single crystal bars; HT-1: single ramp from room temperature to 1,500 K in 20 h followed by air cooling; HT-2: HT-1 followed by additional heat treatment at 1,023 K for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Tensile tests conducted at 298 K, 723 K, 923 K, 1,023 K, and 1,173 K with a constant strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: HESA in HT-2 state achieved a tensile yield strength of 1,023 MPa at 1,023 K, which is 110 MPa higher than CMSX-4.; The cost-specific yield strength of HESA is 8 times that of CMSX-4.; HESA exhibited a tensile elongation greater than 20% at 1,023 K, which is three times greater than that of CMSX-4.; The HT-2 microstructure contains a dispersion of nano-sized disordered FCC particles (4 nm radius, 4.3 vol%) inside ordered L12 precipitates.; The presence of nano HE-FCC particles contributed an estimated 110 MPa increase in yield strength compared to the HT-1 state.; The average L12 precipitate size increased from 143 nm in HT-1 to 153 nm in HT-2.; At 1,173 K, the HE-FCC particles disappeared, and the yield strength of HT-1 and HT-2 states became similar.; The raw material cost of HESA is 84% cheaper than CMSX-4 due to the absence of Re element content.. Mechanism: The formation of nano-sized disordered FCC particles inside the ordered L12 precipitates is driven by the supersaturation of FCC phase formers within the L12 phase during the HT-1 cooling process; these particles act as obstacles that pin superdislocations, increasing the energy required for dislocation motion and thereby enhancing yield strength.. Limitations: The metastable FCC particles inside the L12 phase are thermodynamically unstable and tend to dissolve into the surrounding FCC matrix after prolonged ageing (e.g., 200 h at 1,023 K) or at higher temperatures (1,173 K), leading to a loss of the hierarchical strengthening effect.. Future work: Future alloy design should utilize slow-diffusing species such as Mo to prolong the dissolution rate of FCC particles and improve the thermal stability of the hierarchical microstructure for creep resistance.. Quote: "A hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy layered rare earth hydroxychlorides be synthesized, and how do their structural parameters, elemental distribution, and thermal stability compare to low-entropy analogues?. System: High-entropy layered rare earth hydroxychlorides: (Sm,Eu,Gd,Y,Er)2(OH)5Cl, (Eu,Gd,Tb,Y,Er)2(OH)5Cl, (Eu,Gd,Dy,Y,Er)2(OH)5Cl, (Eu,Gd,Y,Er,Yb)2(OH)5Cl; Medium-entropy: (Eu,Gd,Er)2(OH)5Cl, (Eu,Gd,Y,Er)2(OH)5Cl; Binary/Ternary: EuEr, EuErGd, YEuErGd, Eu_MW, Tb_MW, Er_MW. Processing: Microwave-assisted homogeneous hydrolysis under hydrothermal conditions; 0.1 M REE chloride solutions mixed with 1 M NaCl and 0.14 M hexamethylenetetramine (HMT) at a molar ratio of REE3+:NaCl:HMT = 1:10:1.4; treated in a Teflon autoclave at 140 °C for 30 min (900 W) after 5 min heating at 1800 W; 30% filling degree. Test conditions: XRD (5–90° 2θ, CuKα); EDX mapping (20 kV); FT-IR (3650–3330 cm−1 range); Luminescence (532 nm laser, ~2 mW); Thermal analysis (air, 250 mL/min flow, 20 °C/min heating rate up to 1200 °C). Findings: Unit cell parameters correlate linearly with average rare earth cation radii (0.868 < R2 < 0.982).; Configurational entropy (ΔSconf) for five-cation samples exceeded 1.5R, classifying them as high-entropy compounds.; Ternary and quaternary samples showed ΔSconf between 1R and 1.5R, classifying them as medium-entropy.; EDX mapping confirmed even distribution of rare earth elements on a submicron scale.; Efficient energy transfer between europium and other cations was observed via luminescence quenching or enhancement.; Thermal decomposition occurred in three stages: water elimination (<170 °C), oxide/oxychloride formation (170–700 °C), and chlorine elimination (>1050 °C).; High-entropy samples exhibited thermal stability similar to low-entropy binary and single-cation analogues.; Samples containing Nd3+ showed deviations in unit cell parameters due to impurity phase formation (Nd(OH)3).. Mechanism: The linear correlation between cation radius and unit cell parameters indicates solid solution formation without phase separation. The entropy-stabilization effect is evidenced by the synthesis of single-phase HE_Yb_MW, where single-cation ytterbium hydroxychloride is otherwise unstable. Thermal stability remains comparable to low-entropy systems because the reaction entropy (ΔSdecomp) is not significantly affected by cation composition, as configurational entropy contributes equally to both initial and final decomposition products.. Limitations: The refinement of unit cell parameters for layered rare earth hydroxynitrates is impossible due to stochastic coordination of nitrate anions. Significant differences in cation radii (e.g., in Nd-containing samples) can lead to segregation of individual phases and impurity formation. The study notes that high-entropy layered hydroxides cannot be classified as entropy-stabilized in terms of thermal decomposition.. Future work: The authors suggest that understanding the thermal behavior of metal hydroxides is of primary importance for the synthesis of multicomponent catalytic materials and predicting their functionality.. Quote: "The average rare earth cation radii correlated linearly with the unit cell parameters (0.868 < R2 < 0.982) of the high-entropy layered rare earth hydroxychlorides."

Question: How do phase transformations, thermal expansion, and melting behavior manifest in five-component equimolar rare earth sesquioxide high-entropy alloys compared to their constituent pure oxides?. System: (La,Sm,Dy,Er,RE)2O3 where RE is Nd, Gd, or Y (HE-Nd, HE-Gd, HE-Y). Processing: Solution combustion synthesis followed by annealing at 800 °C for 96 h and 1100 °C for 12 h; laser melting using 400 W CO2 laser on copper hearth or in aerodynamic levitator; splat quenching with ~100 ms drop time; prolonged annealing at 800 °C for 60 days. Test conditions: Differential thermal analysis (DTA) in Ar flow at 20 °C/min up to 2500 °C; high-temperature synchrotron XRD (0.1236 Å wavelength) on laser-heated levitated samples (63–70 mg) with temperature monitoring via pyrometer (emissivity 0.92); room temperature XRD (40 kV, 40 mA, CuKα); electron microprobe analysis (WDS). Findings: All powders annealed at 800 °C contained mainly a C-type bixbyite structure with crystallite sizes of 20–40 nm.; Laser melting followed by splat quenching yielded a single-phase monoclinic B-type structure in all compositions.; Three reversible phase transitions were observed in the range 1900–2400 °C: B-A, A-H, and H-X.; The melting point of the (La,Sm,Dy,Er,Nd)2O3 sample was determined as 2456 ± 12 °C, which is higher than any constituent oxide.; Volume change on C-B transformation was calculated as ~8% in HE-Nd and HE-Gd samples.; Volume change on B-A transition was −2.5 ± 0.1% for HE-Nd and HE-Gd, and −3.1 ± 0.1% for HE-Y.; Volume change on H-X transformation was −1.2 ± 0.1% for HE-Nd and −0.6 ± 0.1% for HE-Y.; Average volume thermal expansion coefficient for the B-type structure was (3.5 ± 0.2) × 10−5/K.. Mechanism: The increase in melting temperature is attributed to nonideal mixing in the solid and/or the melt, specifically negative deviations from ideality in the solid phase (local ordering) or positive deviations in the liquid phase, which favor the solid over the liquid.. Limitations: Calphad predictions for the B-A transformation in HE-Y differed from experiments (predicted direct B-H transition); DTA sensor failure above 2300 °C limited enthalpy/entropy of fusion evaluation; XRD data quality did not allow unambiguous identification of the A-H transition; thermal gradients in laser-heated beads exceed 100 °C.. Future work: Future investigation of the liquidus surface in Sm2O3-Dy2O3, Sm2O3-Er2O3, and Dy2O3-Er2O3 systems is prompted to identify the source of the increased melting temperatures.. Quote: "The melting point was determined for the (La,Sm,Dy,Er,Nd)2O3 sample as 2456 ± 12 °C, which is higher than for any of constituent oxides."

card: Paper card. Question: How can 2D layered high-entropy transition metal hydroxides with homogeneous elemental distribution and designed equimolar stoichiometry be synthesized via a bottom-up soft chemistry method?. System: High-entropy transition metal hydroxides (HEHs) with compositions (Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni, Zn) in equimolar ratios, specifically HEH-1# (CoCrFeMnNi) and HEH-5# (CoFeMnNiZn). Processing: Solvothermal polyol process using ethylene glycol (EG) as solvent, metal nitrate/chloride salts, potassium acetate (KOAC) and/or NaOH as mineralizers, heated at 200 °C for 2 h; post-annealing in air at 200–1000 °C for 2 h with a heating rate of 2 °C min−1. Test conditions: Electrochemical OER testing in 0.1 M KOH electrolyte at 25 °C using a three-electrode system; magnetic measurements via SQUID at 2 K and 300 K; XRD, TEM, EDS, FT-IR, TG-DTA, and ICP-MS characterization. Findings: Interlayer distances of as-synthesized 2D HEHs range from 0.860 to 0.987 nm under EG-K/N conditions.; HEH-5# (CoFeMnNiZn) synthesized under EG-K/N conditions exhibits an overpotential of 275 mV at 10 mA cm−2 for the oxygen evolution reaction.; Annealing at 200 °C converts 2D HEHs into spinel-type nanoparticles with a size of 5 nm and specific surface area of 242.0 m2 g−1.; 600 °C-annealed HEH nanoparticles exhibit superparamagnetic behavior with a blocking temperature of 245 K.; Under EG-K/N conditions, all five metal elements are uniformly distributed in the layered structures with no obvious elemental segregation.; The HEH-5# EG-K/N sample shows better OER performance than HEH-1# due to the substitution of Cr with Zn.; Annealing above 200 °C reduces OER activity due to the collapse of layered structures and increased crystallinity.. Mechanism: The polyol process involves hydrolysis and inorganic polymerization of metal-containing species in ethylene glycol media; the presence of OH− and acetate ions facilitates complexation with metal cations, while the EG solvent inhibits elemental segregation. The formation of high-entropy inorganic–organic hybrid compounds (metal hydroxide acetates) allows co-precipitation of multiple cations at the nanoscale, stabilizing the 2D layered structure. Post-annealing induces decomposition of organic groups and transformation into spinel-type oxides, where entropy stabilization and multi-element synergistic effects contribute to magnetic and catalytic properties.. Limitations: High temperature (>230 °C) or pH (>13) leads to reduction of metal cations by ethylene glycol. The stoichiometry of as-synthesized products can deviate from design if pH is not controlled (e.g., Mn content is lower in EG-K conditions). Some irregularly shaped particles are observed, warranting further optimization of synthesis conditions.. Future work: Further study is required to understand the composition-metal species-magnetic property relationship and to optimize synthesis conditions to eliminate irregular particles. The work opens avenues for synthesizing other low-dimensional functional high-entropy materials such as spinel, pyrochlore, fluorite, perovskite oxides, and layered double hydroxides.. Quote: "Here, we report a simple polyol process for the synthesis of a series of 2D layered high-entropy transition metal (Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni, and Zn) hydroxides (HEHs)"

card: Paper card. Question: Can the dawsonite-type structure (NH4M(OH)2CO3) adapt to a high-entropy form incorporating five or more cations with equimolar and homogeneous distribution?. System: High-entropy dawsonite-type structures with a base of Al, Fe, Cr, Ga and a fifth cation varied by ionic radius (In, Er, Ho, Y, Eu, Ce, La); reference single-cation Al-Dawsonite (Al). Processing: Coprecipitation: Metal nitrate solution (9 mmol total in 40 mL water) added dropwise (6 mL/min) to ammonium bicarbonate solution (0.06 mol in 75 mL water, pH adjusted to 9.5 with NH4OH); stirred overnight (~20 h) at room temperature; centrifuged and dried overnight at 333 K. Test conditions: XRD (Cu Kα, 2θ range); SEM/EDX (20 kV); HAADF-STEM (300 kV); TGA (up to 600 °C, 10 °C/min, synthetic air); FTIR (320–4000 cm–1); N2 adsorption (77 K, degassed at 373 K); Calcination at 523 K; Reconstruction in 1 M (NH4)2CO3 at 323 K. Findings: All high-entropy samples (In, Er, Ho, Y, Ce as fifth cation) showed characteristic dawsonite reflections at 2θ = 15.4°, 26.9°, and 35.1° with no additional phases observed.; EDS mapping confirmed homogeneous distribution of the five cations (In, Al, Fe, Cr, Ga) throughout the particles.; FTIR analysis showed a red-shift of the vOH band from 3434 cm–1 (Al-Daw) to ~3345 cm–1 in multicationic materials.; Thermogravimetric analysis indicated only a 4–8% difference between observed and calculated weight loss, suggesting small amounts of amorphous phase.; High-entropy samples exhibited Type II N2 isotherms, whereas the Al-Daw reference showed a Type IV isotherm with H1 hysteresis.; The high-entropy sample In-AlFeCrGa maintained a specific surface area of 314 m2/g, which increased to 373 m2/g after reconstruction.; Full reconstruction of the dawsonite structure was achieved after calcination at 523 K followed by treatment with ammonium carbonate.; Pure dawsonite-type structures were formed with lanthanides (Ho, Ce, Er) which previously were difficult to incorporate due to mutually exclusive pH regimes.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the structural stability and cation incorporation to the flexibility of the dawsonite-type lattice, noting that the 'many-interaction situation arising from the cation mix and lattice distortions' leads to observed spectral shifts. The memory effect is explained by the ability of the amorphous phase formed at 523 K to completely reconstruct the crystalline dawsonite structure upon exposure to ammonium carbonate solution.. Limitations: The materials are not stable at high temperatures due to their hydrated nature, meaning they may not qualify as 'entropy-stabilized' under certain definitions. Additionally, the high-resolution STEM imaging caused sensitive damage to the multicationic material.. Future work: The authors hypothesize that high-entropy dawsonite-type structures are even more versatile in cation incorporation than demonstrated and suggest that 'under optimized synthesis conditions for specific elements of interest, a wide range of chemistry can be obtained in the high-entropy form.'. Quote: "Through a coprecipitation synthesis method, dawsonite-type materials readily took a high-entropy form with five cations that were equimolar and homogeneously distributed."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti high-entropy alloy be manufactured via Directed Energy Deposition (DED) to achieve a γ + γ′ phase structure that enhances thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength compared to typical FCC-structured HEAs?. System: Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA (45.0 at% Ni, 20.0 at% Co, 10.0 at% Fe, 10.0 at% Cr, 7.5 at% Al, 7.5 at% Ti) deposited on SUS 304 substrates. Processing: Direct Energy Deposition (DED) using a 2 kW diode laser (980 nm, 3 mm beam diameter) with a laser velocity of 10 mm/s, powder feed rate of 7 g/min, hatch spacing of 1 mm, and 11 layers; powders (45 and 150 μm) mixed for 4 hours; nitrogen carrier gas used to prevent oxidation. Test conditions: Room temperature (20 °C) tensile testing per ASTM E8/E8M-18 standard on specimens with 4.5 mm thickness; microhardness measured via Vickers tester with 5 readings per height; XRD (Cu radiation, 40 kV, 50 mA) and EBSD analysis performed. Findings: The alloy exhibited a γ + γ′ phase structure with an ordered FCC (L12) γ′ phase confirmed by XRD superlattice peaks.; Yield strength was measured at 514 MPa and ultimate tensile strength at 605 MPa (631 MPa in conclusions).; Microhardness was consistent at approximately 370 HV across the deposited height.; The average grain size of the γ phase was coarse, measured at 116 μm.; The γ′ phase composition was identified as (Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al) via EDS analysis.; No secondary precipitated phases other than γ + γ′ were detected in the microstructure.; The hardness exceeded that of wrought Inconel 718 (350 HV).. Mechanism: The addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within the multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, where the ordered FCC γ′ phase significantly improves mechanical properties, thermal stability, and coarsening resistance.. Limitations: The tensile strength is lower than Inconel 718 due to the coarsening of the microstructure caused by high-temperature deposition, and the grain size distribution is uneven due to variations in processing parameters and cooling rates.. Future work: Post-processing treatments like heat treatment are expected to refine the phase size and improve mechanical properties; precise phase analysis and post-treatment procedures should be added to further advance the manufacturing method.. Quote: "The γ′ phase with an ordered FCC structure significantly improves the mechanical properties."

card: Paper card. Question: How do additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and post-heat treatments influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and deformation mechanisms of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) compared to conventional casting methods?. System: CoCrFeNi, AlxCoCrFeNi (x=0.3, 0.6, 0.85), CoCrFeMnNi, FeCoCrAlCu, Ti25Zr50Nb0Ta25, CoCrFeNiTi, and AA5083/CoCrFeNi composites. Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD/DMD/DLF), and Selective Electron Beam Melting (SEBM); parameters include layer thickness (20–100 μm), volumetric energy density (VED), laser power (e.g., 400 W), scanning speed (e.g., 1200 mm/s), and pre-heating; post-treatments include High Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1100 °C for 2 h, annealing (750–1000 °C), and solution treatment.. Test conditions: Tensile and compression tests at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K); microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EBSD; wear resistance testing.. Findings: AM-processed HEAs exhibit superior yield strength and ductility compared to casting counterparts due to fine microstructures formed by rapid solidification.; SLM CoCrFeNi specimens showed significantly higher yield strength than arc-melt specimens while retaining significant ductility.; Increasing volumetric energy density (VED) in SLM CoCrFeMnNi reduced holes and cracks, leading to higher ultimate tensile strength.; HIP treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h removed second-phase grain-boundary phases and segregation in Al0.3CoCrFeNi, achieving chemical homogenization.; SEBM AlCoCrFeNi specimens displayed better plasticity than cast specimens due to finer grains and a substantial fraction of ductile FCC phase.; Cryogenic testing (77 K) on LAM-fabricated CrMnFeCoNi HEA enhanced yield strength and ductility, with deformation twinning becoming more obvious at high strain.; Solution treatment of SEBM CoCrFeNiTi HEA improved ductility without lowering strength by removing needle-like Ni3Ti precipitates.; Different AM methods induce substantial differences in yield strength and plasticity; for instance, DLF Al0.3CoCrFeNi showed much lower yield strength compared to SLM and SEBM methods.. Mechanism: The enhanced mechanical properties are primarily ascribed to the refinement of microstructures caused by large temperature gradients and rapid solidification during AM, which leads to fine cellular dendrite structures, high dislocation densities, and suppressed elemental segregation. Post-treatments like HIP and annealing further enhance properties by removing fabrication defects (pores, microcracks) and releasing residual stress, while specific heat treatments can dissolve or modify precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti, B2 phases) to optimize the balance between strength and ductility.. Limitations: Defects such as residual stress, microcracks, and pores exist in as-built AM components, degrading mechanical properties; some AM specimens exhibit anisotropy in mechanical properties due to texture and grain orientation; limited ductility is observed in some Al-rich alloys due to brittle phase appearance; most existing studies focus on tension/compression, with rare data on fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, or corrosion.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters and heat treatment regimes to improve microstructures and reduce residual stress; investigate fracture toughness, fatigue, oxidation, irradiation, and corrosion properties; expand research to light-weight and refractory HEAs; develop broader compositional ranges; investigate materials with large differences in melting temperatures; and study effective powder blending methods to reduce agglomeration and increase homogeneity.. Quote: "Compared with the casting counterparts, AM-HEAs were found to have a superior yield strength and ductility as a consequence of the fine microstructure formed during the rapid solidification in the fabrication process."

Question: How do simultaneous microalloying with carbon (C) and molybdenum (Mo) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties of Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloys?. System: [Co40Cr25(FeNi)35−yMoy]100−xCx (x = 0, 0.5; y = 3, 4, 5 at.%) HEAs. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of pure elements (≥99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, melted five times for homogeneity, solution treated at 1200 °C for 2 h, water quenched, and hot rolled with 70% reduction. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; XRD (20° to 100°, 40 kV, 40 mA); SEM and EBSD analysis. Mechanism: The superior mechanical properties of the Mo4C0.5 alloy are attributed to a combination of fine grain strengthening, interstitial solid solution strengthening from carbon, precipitation strengthening from carbides, and the TWIP effect where deformation twins hinder dislocation slip, delay necking, and enhance work hardening.. card: Paper card. Question: How can integrated computational material engineering (ICME) and machine learning be used to design single-phase ordered B2 aluminum-enriched refractory high-entropy alloys (Al-RHEAs) that achieve a synergy of high strength and ductility, and what is the fundamental role of valence electron count (VEC) and long-range ordering (LRO) in this process?. System: Al-Hf-Nb-Ti-V quaternary and quinary systems, specifically Al25Hf25Nb25Ti25, Al20Hf24Nb29Ti27, Al15Hf25Nb32Ti28, and Al10Hf20Nb22Ti33V15. Processing: Arc melting of high-purity raw elements (>99.99 wt %) in a water-cooled copper crucible using a 400-A current for 30 s per melt (at least five melts with flipping), followed by suction casting into copper molds for compression testing and TEM sample preparation. Test conditions: Compression tests at an initial strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; tensile tests at an initial strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1; high-temperature compression up to 700°C. Findings: Al25Hf25Nb25Ti25 achieved a compressive yield strength of ~1.7 GPa but a low fracture strain of ~2% due to strong B2 long-range ordering (LRO).; Reducing Al content to 20 at % (Al20Hf24Nb29Ti27) increased the fracture strain to 35% while maintaining a yield strength of 1.6 GPa, attributed to weakened B2-LRO.; Further reducing Al to 15 at % (Al15Hf25Nb32Ti28) resulted in a yield strength of 1.5 GPa and exceptional plasticity, with samples enduring up to 50% height reduction without fracture.; The quinary alloy Al10Hf20Nb22Ti33V15 exhibited a tensile yield strength of 1.0 GPa with a ductility of 9%, representing the first single B2 phase Al-RHEA with tensile ductility in the as-cast condition.; High-temperature compression of Al10Hf20Nb22Ti33V15 maintained a yield strength above 800 MPa at 700°C.; MC simulations showed that decreasing Al content lowers the order-disorder transformation temperature (Ttransform) from ~2000 K to ~750 K, reducing the extent of LRO established during solidification.; A 'VEC valley' of brittleness was identified between VEC 5.5 and 6.2, where alloys exhibit low ductility due to high covalency and low density of states at the Fermi level.; The Al10Hf20Nb22Ti33V15 alloy showed a faint B2 ordering observable only by TEM, with an estimated LRO of ~33% of the reference state at 0 K.. Mechanism: The authors argue that strong B2 long-range ordering (LRO) hinders dislocation movement, increasing strength but reducing ductility. Reducing Al content lowers the order-disorder transformation temperature (Ttransform), limiting LRO development during solidification and facilitating plastic deformation via <111> dislocation glide. Additionally, the 'VEC valley' of brittleness (5.5–6.2) is explained by a low density of states at the Fermi level (D(EF)), which increases covalency and shear modulus, promoting brittleness; avoiding this VEC range is crucial for ductility.. Limitations: The authors state that the current ML models for predicting compressive yield strength and fracture strain are not ambitious in obtaining precise predictions for B2 Al-RHEAs due to database noise and the baseline model being trained on disordered BCC alloys. They also note that achieving the MC-predicted equilibrium state at low temperatures is nearly impossible due to sluggish atomic diffusion.. Future work: The authors propose that continued research into mechanical and thermal treatments is anticipated to refine the microstructure and further enhance ductility. They also suggest that the hypothesis regarding strain-induced reduction of LRO during plastic deformation needs experimental verification, such as in situ neutron diffraction.. Quote: "Ultrastrong and ductile alloys were designed by an integrated computation model and "VEC valley" for brittleness was uncovered."

Processing: High-throughput Monte Carlo simulations on a fixed BCC lattice using binary interaction energies derived from an enthalpy matrix; experimental validation via in situ neutron scattering (room temp to 1600°C using aerodynamic levitation), in situ STEM heating (room temp to 700°C), and DSC (cooling at 20°C/min from 1450 to 250°C). Test conditions: Simulations: cooling from high temperatures; Neutron scattering: 300 K to 1600°C; STEM: 300 K to 700°C; DSC: 1450°C to 250°C at 20°C/min. Findings: The ordering onset temperature (Tc) is strongly dependent on Al content, ranging from approximately 1220 °C for x = 1 to 1850 °C for x = 2.; In Al2CoCrFeNi (x=2), the B2 phase remains strongly ordered at the melting point, whereas in AlCoCrFeNi (x=1), B2 order is lost near 1400 °C.; A sharp transformation involving phase separation occurs near 600 °C for all compositions between x = 1 and 2.; Below 600 °C, the B2 phase is primarily composed of Ni, Co, and Al, while the disordered phase is primarily composed of Fe and Cr.; The fraction of Al-Al pairs decreases as Al content increases, indicating significant short-range order around Al atoms even in the high-temperature disordered BCC phase.; DSC measurements on AlCoCrFeNi show a peak near 575 °C, consistent with the simulated transformation temperature of 565 ± 30 °C.; In situ STEM reveals that Cr-Fe-enriched plate-like microstructures decompose upon heating to 600 °C, with complete breakdown into globular Cr-rich regions by 700 °C.. Mechanism: The phase evolution is driven by the strong ordering tendencies of Al with transition metals (particularly Ni and Co) leading to B2 formation, followed by a temperature-dependent separation where weakly interacting elements (Cr, Fe) precipitate into a disordered BCC solid solution while Al, Ni, and Co remain in the ordered B2 sublattices; this is modeled via nearest-neighbor interactions on a rigid lattice where configurational entropy decreases during cooling.. Limitations: The lattice-constrained simulations neglect the possibility of changing the underlying lattice and ignore potential vibrational entropy effects associated with small displacements from the average position; the limited length scales in simulations may prevent a full description of the behavior.. Future work: The approach provides a simple method to guide the development of ordered multi-phase HEAs for structural applications and suggests a broader strategy for rapid exploration of phase evolution where little experimental data exists.. Quote: "Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases"

card: Paper card. Question: Can binary phase diagrams be used to predict the phase formation (single solid solution, mixed phases, or intermetallics) of high entropy alloys (HEAs) through a phenomenological method combined with machine learning?. System: 614 reported HEAs (Level 3) and 42 newly synthesized complex compositions containing 4 to 7 elements from refractory metals, transition metals, and main group elements (e.g., Al2CoCrCuNi). Processing: Suction casting of master ingots (arc-melted 3 times in high purity argon, 99.7 wt% purity elements) into 3 mm diameter rods; annealing at temperatures > 0.7 Tm for some database entries; phase formation temperature (Tpf) optimized at 0.8 Tm for as-cast alloys. Test conditions: X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis using Cu Kα radiation; Machine Learning classification using Random Forest with 300 trees and 2-10 fold cross-validation on 614 HEAs; validation on 42 new compositions. Findings: The model achieved an overall HEA prediction success rate above 80% and a single-phase HEA prediction rate above 80%.; Validation on 42 randomly selected complex compositions yielded a success rate of 81% (34 out of 42 predicted correctly).; Level 1 (disordered phases) single phase predictions had success rates of 89–90% for as-cast HEAs.; Level 2 (including B2 + SS) overall and B2 + SS phase prediction success rates were near 85%.; Level 3 (including IM+ phases) overall success rate was 80%, with IM+ phase prediction rates of 73–78%.; High accuracy was maintained even with training set percentages as low as 50%.; The optimized phase formation temperature (Tpf) for as-cast HEAs was determined to be 0.8 Tm.. Mechanism: The authors hypothesize that HEA structural stability is encoded within binary phase diagrams; they use phase field percentages at a specific temperature (Tpf) and a phase separation parameter (PSP) to quantify the tendency of constituent binary pairs to form specific phases, which are then combined combinatorially to predict multi-component alloy phases.. Limitations: The study excludes minor phases such as line compounds; mechanically alloyed HEAs are not included because ball milling tends to retain metastable phases; the model's performance slightly abates when annealed HEAs are added to the as-cast set.. Future work: The authors propose including additional physical parameters (e.g., mixing enthalpy) into the ML to improve accuracy, and interacting with other models like CALPHAD where the current model serves as a fast screening tool for in-depth thermodynamic studies.. Quote: "For the first time, a phenomenological method analysing binary phase diagrams to predict HEA phases is presented."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to identify lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys in the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system that maintain structural stability and high strength at elevated temperatures?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 identified as successful LWHEAs). Processing: High-throughput CALPHAD-based computational screening (3246 alloys calculated with 5 at.% step size) followed by arc-melting of eight selected alloys with 99.9 wt% purity elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, and drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific samples.. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 700 °C (strain rate 2 × 10−4 s−1); in situ neutron diffraction during uniaxial compression; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD; TEM and APT characterizations.. Findings: Eight alloys were identified from 3246 initial compositions meeting criteria for Tm > 1250 °C and specific L21 phase fractions (0.05–0.5) at 0.5Tm and 0.8Tm.; Alloy 1 (Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5) exhibited a yield strength of 1072 ± 25 MPa at 600 °C and 607 ± 22 MPa at 700 °C.; Alloy 1 contained high-density nanoscaled L21 precipitates (10–30 nm) with a number density of 2.76 × 10^22/m^3 and volume fraction of 43.6 vol.%.; Alloys 2–7 formed ordered L21 antiphase domains (APDs) with ~85 vol.% fraction, behaving like a single L21 phase rather than a precipitation-strengthened composite.; The ordering transition temperature (Tc) for Alloy 1 was calculated at 1607 °C, significantly lower than Alloy 7's Tc of 1997 °C.; Precipitation strengthening in Alloy 1 contributed ~904 MPa to the yield strength, attributed to ordering strengthening.; Alloy 1 showed clear load-transfer behavior in neutron diffraction, whereas Alloy 7 showed synchronized lattice strain response indicating single-phase behavior.. Mechanism: The formation of nanoscale L21 precipitates versus antiphase domains is governed by the deviation of chemical composition from the perfect L21 stoichiometry (Fe2AlTi-type). Alloys with compositions deviating from stoichiometry (G1) form precipitates within a BCC matrix, enabling precipitation strengthening via load transfer. Alloys matching stoichiometry (G2) form a single-phase L21 structure with APDs. The order-disorder transition temperature is controlled by atomic-site occupancy and interaction energies (e.g., Fe–Al, Fe–Ti pairs favor L21; Cr–Fe pairs favor BCC), where lower Tc allows retention of the BCC matrix alongside L21 precipitates.. Limitations: The current thermodynamic database requires improvement regarding the stability of the L21 phase, as evidenced by the microstructure discrepancy between prediction and observation for Alloys 2–7. The high-throughput predictions are currently valid only in the composition range of Al < 25 at.% and Mn > 15 at.% with unchanged contents of other elements.. Future work: Long-period annealing on the identified alloys and quantitative characterization are necessary to improve the thermodynamic database. The high-throughput design method should be coupled with the deciphered atomic occupancy rules to accelerate the discovery of advanced HEAs, particularly for multicomponent systems.. Quote: "Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy nanoparticles be synthesized rapidly and cost-effectively in a solid-phase without phase separation, and what are the underlying mechanisms involving laser interaction with precursors and supports?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles encapsulated by graphene shells, synthesized on 3D porous laser-induced graphene (LIG) from polybenzimidazole (PBI) on carbon paper; also extended to CrMnFeCoNi oxide, sulfide, and phosphide.. Processing: Dissolved equal-molar metal chlorides (CrCl3·6H2O, MnCl2, FeCl3, CoCl2·6H2O, NiCl2·6H2O) in ethanol/water; immersed LIG-coated carbon paper in solutions (1–20 mM); dried at 80 °C for 30 min; irradiated with Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm, 30 ns pulse width, 10 kHz repetition rate) under Ar atmosphere at scanning rates of 2000 mm/s and fluences of 58.9–96.8 mJ/cm2.. Test conditions: Electrocatalytic testing in 1 M KOH alkaline media; OER performance evaluated via LSV, Tafel analysis, and chronopotentiometry at current densities of 10–200 mA/cm2; stability tested for 428 h at 10 mA/cm2; temperature measured up to 2000 °C via infrared camera and simulated via ABAQUS.. Findings: Production rate reached 30 g/h (specifically 29.6 g/h reported in text) under the current laser setup.; CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles achieved an average size of ~15 nm (uniform between 0.005–0.015 M precursor concentration) and FCC solid solution structure.; Overpotential of 293 mV at 10 mA/cm2 for OER, outperforming commercial RuO2 (312 mV).; Tafel slope of 57.9 mV/dec for IE-HEA/LIG versus 83.1 mV/dec for commercial RuO2.; Exceptional stability over 428 h with only a 74 mV potential increase, whereas RuO2 disintegrated within 2 h.; Localized surface temperature reached 1960 K experimentally and simulated up to 2381 K with a cooling rate of 10^7 K/s.; Thermionic emission current reached 0.15 μA at 3 kV bias voltage under laser irradiation.; Mn content was lower than Fe, Co, and Ni due to partial vaporization (boiling point 2334 K) during synthesis.. Mechanism: The synthesis proceeds via laser-induced photothermal decomposition of metal precursors and reduction by thermionic electrons emitted from the LIG support. Laser energy is absorbed by LIG, generating heat that conducts to precursors causing decomposition, while hot electrons reduce metal ions to atoms. Molten beads form above melting temperatures but are split into smaller droplets by laser-induced high pressure, followed by rapid solidification. The graphene layers bend to encapsulate the nanoparticles, preventing aggregation.. Limitations: The text notes that the boiling temperature of Mn (2334 K) is close to the highest laser-induced temperature, leading to partial evaporation and non-equimolar composition (lower Mn content). Additionally, the disintegration of the carbon paper support was observed after 200 h due to rapid oxygen gas evolution, though less severe than with RuO2.. Future work: The authors state the technique demonstrates versatility for synthesizing HEA oxide, sulfide, and phosphide nanoparticles, suggesting further exploration of nonmetallic atom incorporation to induce lattice distortion and enhance performance. They also propose the method as an industrially viable solution for scalable manufacturing of composition-tunable nanomaterials.. Quote: "The production rate reaches up to 30 g/h under the current laser setup."
