card: Paper card. Question: How can uniformly dispersed high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) be synthesized on granular supports (e.g., carbon, Al2O3, zeolite) without phase separation, overcoming the limitations of conventional fixed-bed pyrolysis?. System: Denary (MnCoNiCuRhPdSnIrPtAu), quinary (FeCoPdIrPt, CuPdSnPtAu), and other multi-element (up to 10 elements) HEA-NPs supported on graphene oxide (GO), carbon black, γ-Al2O3, and zeolite (Permutit). Processing: Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) following wet impregnation: Metal chlorides coordinated with 1,10-Phenanthroline loaded on supports; quartz boat pushed into a 923 K furnace zone at 20 cm s−1 (reaching 923 K within 5 s); annealing for 120 min at 923 K under Ar (100 sccm) or H2 (100 sccm) for oxide supports. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in 1 M KOH (pH 13.8) at 10 mA cm−2 and 100 mA cm−2; stability tested via chronopotentiometry for 150 h; structural characterization via HR-STEM, HAADF-STEM, EDX, XRD, XPS, and ICP-OES. Findings: HEA-NPs achieved a narrow size distribution of ~2 nm up to denary compositions at 923 K; FMBP ensures simultaneous pyrolysis of mixed precursors, preventing phase separation unlike fixed-bed pyrolysis (FBP) which yields phase-separated alloys; FeCoPdIrPt@GO exhibited an overpotential of 42 mV at 10 mA cm−2, lower than commercial Pt/C (64 mV); Mass activity of FeCoPdIrPt@GO at 100 mV overpotential was 9.1 mA μgPt, 26 times higher than Pt/C (0.35 mA μgPt); Long-term stability of 150 h maintained at 10 mA cm−2 with no obvious change in morphology or composition; Atomic ratio error in synthesized alloys was below 15%, confirmed by EDX and ICP-OES; Tafel slope for FeCoPdIrPt was 82 mV dec−1, indicating the fastest kinetics among tested samples. Mechanism: The rapid heating to 923 K within 5 s creates high supersaturation of monomers, leading to a small critical nucleus radius (r* = 0.313 nm) and low critical excess free energy (ΔGr* = 2.54 × 10−20 J). This thermodynamically favors the formation of small, homogeneous nuclei clusters without phase separation, whereas slower heating (FBP/SMBP) results in larger nuclei and phase segregation due to higher ΔGr*.. Limitations: The text notes that HEA-NPs with low loading (3 wt%) were too small for clear EDX mapping, requiring higher loading (10 wt%) for elemental analysis; also, annealing times of 30 min led to carbon wrapping, while 180 min caused significant particle growth.. Future work: The authors propose a scalable method for production of supported HEA-NPs and suggest the strategy opens a venue for synthesizing alloys with tunable compositions for applications in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion.. Quote: "Fast moving bed pyrolysis strategy ensures the mixed metal precursors rapidly and simultaneously pyrolyzed at high temperatures, resulting in nuclei with a small size."

card: Paper card. Question: How can colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters below 5 nm be synthesized in a single step, and can this process be scaled for industrial application?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (equimolar composition). Processing: Single-step liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals; low-power system: 10 ps Nd:YAG laser, 1064 nm, 100 kHz, 8.8 W, ethanol solvent, 20 mL min⁻¹ flow; high-power system: 3 ps laser, 1030 nm, 10 MHz, water solvent, 500 mL min⁻¹ flow, scanning speed 484 m s⁻¹. Test conditions: Electrochemical analysis in 0.1 M NaOH (pH 13) using a three-electrode setup with Pt counter electrode and Ag/AgCl reference; potentials corrected to RHE; linear sweep voltammetry at 20 mV s⁻¹ with electrode rotation at 1600 rpm; current densities extracted at 1.7 V vs. RHE. Findings: Colloidal HEA nanoparticles with diameters less than 5 nm were successfully synthesized, with ultrasmall NPs (2.8 nm) making up the main product by number, surface, and volume.; The process demonstrated unprecedented scalability with a productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour using the high-power laser system.; The chemical composition of the nanoparticles was nearly equimolar, preserving the target stoichiometry without selective ablation of single elements.; The crystal lattice of the nanoparticles was preserved as a single fcc structure, matching the bulk HEA target, as confirmed by XRD, SAED, and HRTEM.; The synthesized nanoparticles exhibited unique redox behavior in an alkaline environment, with mass activities of 0.104 A mg⁻¹ at 1.7 V vs. RHE for water-based synthesis.; Surface segregation of Cr and Mn was observed in larger NPs (>50 nm) due to longer residence times in the low-density mixing region, leading to minor spinel oxide formation.; The synthesis process was highly reproducible, with variations of less than 10% in productivity and size distribution, and up to 12% deviation in catalytic performance.. Mechanism: The formation mechanism involves laser irradiation creating a plume and cavitation bubble; ablated species mix with liquid vapor in a supercritical state, cool rapidly (cooling rates ~10¹² K s⁻¹), and condense into NPs. Ultrasmall NPs form via nucleation and condensation in the low-density mixing region, while larger NPs emerge from a molten layer due to Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Surface segregation and oxidation occur in a late stage for larger NPs with longer residence times, while smaller NPs cool too fast for segregation.. Limitations: The presence of a minor spinel oxide phase and surface segregation of Cr and Mn in larger NPs; the complexity of assigning specific redox features to individual metals in the multi-element system; and the lack of direct quantitative surface analysis (e.g., XPS) to confirm surface compositions.. Future work: The authors propose varying the composition of the CoCrFeMnNi alloy to identify the most active composition for catalysis, extending quantitative and structural analysis of NP surfaces to investigate the origin of catalytic performance, and utilizing the method for rapid screening of different functional materials by varying alloy composition, liquid environment, and immobilization substrate.. Quote: "Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals."

Processing: Two-step method: (1) Mechanical milling of 4 g graphite powder with elemental blend (0.193 g Fe, 0.180 g Cr, 0.204 g Co, 0.220 g Cu, 0.203 g Ni) in toluene for 80 hours with a 20:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio; (2) Sonication of the milled composite in 10 ml ethanol with 20 mg sodium lauryl sulphate (SLS) for 2 hours, followed by centrifugation at 8000 rpm to remove SLS.. Test conditions: Electrochemical corrosion testing in 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature using a three-electrode cell (working electrode: HEA-Gr/epoxy coated mild steel, counter: platinum foil, reference: Ag/AgCl); potentiodynamic polarization from ±200 mV vs OCP at 1 mVs⁻¹; EIS from 100 kHz to 0.01 Hz with 5 mV amplitude.. Findings: Average nanoparticle size was 8 ± 2 nm with an average graphene thickness of 3.3 ± 0.9 nm.; The nanoparticles exhibited a face centred cubic (fcc) structure with a lattice parameter of 3.394 Å.; Total polarization resistance (Rp) for the HEA-Gr composite-epoxy coating was 19650 Ω, significantly higher than bare MS (903.9 Ω) and graphene-epoxy coated MS (5843 Ω).; The HEA-Gr composite showed a positive shift in corrosion potential (Ecorr) and decreased corrosion current density (Icorr) compared to all control samples.; STEM-EDS analysis confirmed all five component metal atoms (Fe, Cr, Co, Cu, Ni) were uniformly distributed within individual nanoparticles.; A large distribution in composition between individual nanoparticles was observed, with Ni present in the lowest amount in a large fraction of particles.. Mechanism: Strain caused by the presence of nanoparticles within the inter-layer spacing of graphite facilitated the exfoliation process during sonication. The resulting HEA nanoparticles form a protective layer that significantly reduces surface activity towards the corrosion environment, enhancing the barrier properties beyond what graphene alone provides.. Limitations: The text notes a large distribution in the composition between the nanoparticles, with Cr showing a relatively wider distribution and Ni often present in the lowest amounts, suggesting compositional heterogeneity at the single-particle level.. Future work: The authors propose that the as-synthesised HEA nanoparticle-graphene composite can be spray painted over surfaces to provide enhanced corrosion protection.. Quote: "Strain caused due to the presence of nanoparticles within the inter-layer spacing facilitated the exfoliation process during the subsequent sonication of the multimetal-graphite powder resulting in the formation of HEA nanoparticle decorated graphene."
